paper_topic: Fielded max-sim keying for assistant-side memory recall in long-term conversational assistants

nodes.text: Long-term conversational assistants must recall information from extensive interaction histories spanning weeks or months (Packer et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2023).

As these histories grow beyond context window limits, retrieval-augmented approaches become essential: given a user query, the system retrieves relevant past conversation rounds to inform its response (Gao et al., 2023).
The effectiveness of such memory systems depends critically on how conversation rounds are indexed for retrieval.
Current conversational memory systems predominantly index only user utterances, treating each round's user turn as the retrieval key (Maharana et al., 2024).
nodes.display_label: Current systems index user utterances only

nodes.text: This design reflects an implicit assumption that users query about information they previously provided.
nodes.display_label: Assumes users query own past info

nodes.text: However, the LongMemEval benchmark (Wu et al., 2024) identifies a distinct category of queries—single-session-assistant (SSA) questions—where users ask about information the assistant provided in earlier turns, such as "What restaurant did you recommend last week?"
For SSA queries, the relevant information resides in assistant responses, creating a fundamental mismatch with user-only indexing.
A natural solution is to concatenate user and assistant text into a single embedding.
However, this approach suffers from cross-field interference: mixing semantically different content in one embedding dilutes query-relevant features.

Our experiments confirm this hypothesis—concatenation improves SSA recall but causes catastrophic degradation on other query types (−0.145 overall Recall@10), making it unsuitable for production deployment.
We propose fielded max-sim keying, which treats each conversation round as a two-field document with separate embeddings for user and assistant content.
The relevance score is the maximum similarity across fields, providing a natural field selection mechanism: user-centric queries match the user field while SSA queries match the assistant field.
This approach requires no additional training—only a change in indexing and scoring.

We demonstrate a zero-harm property: fielded max-sim achieves identical overall Recall@10 (0.664) to user-only indexing while improving SSA Recall@10 by +0.018 and NDCG@10 by +0.038, enabling risk-free adoption as a drop-in replacement.

We provide empirical evidence of cross-field interference in concatenation-based indexing, which degrades overall Recall@10 by −0.145 despite improving SSA recall, explaining why naive field combination fails.
We compare max-sim against linear mixture scoring and show that only the non-linear max operator achieves zero-harm—linear mixtures trade SSA gains for unacceptable overall degradation.

observations:
FA0153 follows a two-pivot Prior_Work to Limitation arc framing the assistant-side recall problem. Para 1 (N1-N3) is pure Context: long-term assistants need recall, retrieval-augmented memory is essential, and indexing is the critical lever. Para 2 introduces the first Prior_Work (N4-N5: current systems index user utterances only, assuming users query their own past info), then pivots via 'However' to a Limitation pair (N6-N7) — LongMemEval surfaces SSA queries that break the user-only assumption.

Para 3 introduces a second, weaker Prior_Work (N8: concatenation as natural solution), pivots via 'However' to a second Limitation (N9: cross-field interference), and N10 is a Result-as-evidence: an experimental number (-0.145 overall Recall@10) that quantifies the concatenation failure. The Method block (N11-N13) proposes fielded max-sim keying — the field-selection insight (N12) and training-free property (N13) are explicit elaborations of the proposal.

Three Contributions (C1-C3) close the intro. Three addresses edges link them back: C1 (zero-harm) addresses the SSA mismatch limitation N7; C2 (empirical cross-field interference) addresses the concatenation interference limitation N9; C3 (max beats linear mixtures) also addresses N9 since it speaks to the same alternative-method failure mode. Topology features two parallel Prior_Work to Limitation contrast pivots and a contribution-fan from N13. Both Limitations N6/N7 are sourced from the user-only Prior_Work cluster (N4/N5), and N9 is sourced from N8, satisfying the PW->Limitation rule everywhere.
